text: In New York he bought fine clothes, silk underwear, and silver mounted brushes, and he took rooms at the Waldorf, explaining that he was from Washington and that his parents were abroad. <break time="0.8s" /> Surrounded by flowers, soft carpets, and music drifting up from the dining room, he felt that this was exactly what all the struggle of his life had been about. <break time="0.8s" /> One night he went out with a wild boy from San Francisco, a freshman at Yale, and they stayed out until dawn, but in the morning they parted singularly cool. <break time="0.8s" /> He felt no remorse, for here, as he glanced down at his dress coat, he was sure that it would be impossible for anyone to humiliate him. <break time="0.8s" /> On the eighth morning he found his own story in a Pittsburgh paper, which reported that his father had repaid the money and was coming to New York to bring him home. <break time="0.8s" /> The gray monotony of Cordelia Street stretched before him in hopeless, unrelieved years of Sunday school, yellow wallpaper, and damp dish towels, and he could not bear it. <break time="0.8s" /> He left the city and wandered out into the snowy country beside the railroad, where the red carnations in his coat had already drooped and lost their glory in the cold. <break time="0.8s" /> It seemed to him that the flowers had had only one splendid breath, for all their brave mockery at the winter, and he buried one of them gently in the snow. <break time="0.8s" /> When the train came near through the falling snow, Paul stepped toward it, and there Cather ends his story, letting him drop back into the immense design of things.
